explanation: Fat loss is often inferred from scale weight, but scale weight is only a proxy.
Repeated weigh-ins create a bodyweight trend.
Expected loss is compared with observed loss to identify whether the scale is behaving as expected.
Observed loss is compared with expected loss to quantify the gap.
A sustained calorie deficit should create expected weight loss over time.
Calorie intake is one side of the energy balance equation.
Energy expenditure is the other side of the energy balance equation.
Steps are a practical proxy for non-exercise activity.
NEAT contributes to total daily energy expenditure.
Structured training contributes to energy expenditure.
Exercise energy expenditure forms part of total calories out.
Consistent protein intake can support satiety and diet quality.
Consistent calorie intake can indicate stronger adherence.
Incomplete or inaccurate logging can make apparent deficits unreliable.
Large weekend calorie differences may indicate adherence drift.
If intake is inconsistent, expected loss may be overestimated.
Higher carbohydrate intake can increase glycogen storage.
Glycogen storage is associated with water storage.
Water retention can temporarily hide fat loss on the scale.
Gut content can alter short-term scale weight independently of fat loss.
Sleep affects recovery from training and dieting.
Lower sleep quality can reduce recovery readiness.
Higher stress can reduce recovery capacity.
Higher training load increases recovery demand.
Poor recovery may increase weight volatility and water retention.
Higher short-term weight volatility supports the idea that scale weight may be masking fat loss.
Water retention is a primary mechanism behind masked fat loss.
A mismatch between expected and observed loss can look like a plateau.
A mismatch can indicate that fat loss is occurring but being hidden.
A drop in steps may suggest reduced expenditure.
Reduced expenditure can shrink the actual deficit and explain poor observed loss.
Recovery stress can contribute to water retention and masked fat loss.
A true plateau is a more persistent form of plateau where masking explanations are less likely.
Higher training load can increase muscle damage, inflammation and short-term fluid retention.
Training-related inflammation can temporarily increase water retention and mask fat loss.
Training inflammation supports a recovery-driven water retention explanation.
Higher or inconsistent sodium intake can increase short-term water retention.
Sodium inconsistency supports a dietary water retention explanation.
Changes in carbohydrate intake can alter glycogen storage.
Carbohydrate shifts influence glycogen storage.
Large carbohydrate shifts can support a dietary water retention explanation.
Poor sleep duration can reduce recovery quality.
Poor subjective sleep quality can reduce recovery quality.
Poor sleep recovery reduces overall recovery readiness.
Poor sleep recovery supports a recovery-driven water retention explanation.
Higher stress load can tax recovery capacity.
Stress load supports a recovery-driven water retention explanation.
Alcohol can reduce sleep quality and disturb recovery.
Alcohol intake can support a dietary or lifestyle-driven water retention explanation.
Higher digestive load can increase gut content and short-term scale weight.
Digestive mass can increase scale weight independently of fat gain.
Illness or immune stress can increase water retention and distort scale weight.
Illness-related inflammation supports a recovery-driven water retention explanation.
Recovery-driven water retention can explain why fat loss is hidden on the scale.
Dietary water retention can explain short-term scale weight masking.
